description: SMIDGE is a space mission design game developed to help a broad audience understand the principles of space mission planning, as well as the scientific and technical efforts involved in the process.
summary: SMIDGE, which stands for Space Mission Interactive Design and Game Environment, is an interactive space mission design game set on a low Earth orbit space station inspired by the International Space Station (ISS). Players first act as mission engineers, selecting equipment cards related to power, air, water and food supply, protection, and crew health. Every card has a cost, a mass, a power draw, and a real tradeoff, so a limited budget and launch mass force hard choices. Then the player becomes the crew, flying a 2D astronaut through the station they designed while managing oxygen, CO₂, power, water, and crew health. The simulation introduces random emergencies such as debris impacts, solar radiation events, and equipment malfunctions, which must be fixed before they cause damage. A final scorecard evaluates the mission with a letter grade and bases it on survival, resources, response time, and budget and mass efficiency, so players see how each early decision shaped the outcome. The game turns abstract engineering tradeoffs into something students can experience firsthand. Numbers and events are based on NASA statistics simplified for gameplay.
details:
SMIDGE — Space Mission Interactive Design and Game Environment

Project Overview

SMIDGE is an interactive space mission design game based on a low Earth orbit space station inspired by the International Space Station (ISS).

The game combines:

  • Aerospace engineering
  • Resource management
  • Mission planning
  • Interactive astronaut gameplay

Its goal is to teach players how engineering decisions affect the operation and survival of a space station.

How It Works

The game has two main phases:

Phase 1: Mission Engineering

Players design their own space station by selecting equipment in different categories:

  • Power generation and distribution
  • Air and life-support systems
  • Water and food supplies
  • Radiation and debris protection
  • Crew health and safety

Each piece of equipment has:

  • Cost
  • Mass
  • Power consumption
  • Advantages and disadvantages

Players must stay within budget and launch-mass limits while prioritizing essential systems.

Phase 2: Crew Operations

Players take control of a 2D astronaut aboard their completed station.

They must monitor and maintain:

  • Oxygen and carbon dioxide
  • Electrical power
  • Water supplies
  • Crew health

Unexpected events can also occur, such as equipment failures, orbital debris impacts, and solar radiation events. Players must respond before these problems threaten the mission.

At the end, a scoring system evaluates the mission based on survival, resource management, emergency response, and engineering efficiency.

Benefits and Intended Impact

SMIDGE makes aerospace engineering more accessible by allowing players to experience the consequences of their decisions.

The game encourages:

  • Critical thinking and problem-solving
  • Understanding spacecraft life-support systems
  • Resource and budget management
  • Engineering tradeoff analysis
  • Decision-making under pressure

The goal is to increase interest in aerospace engineering and STEM while introducing players to the challenges of NASA mission design.

Tools and Development

The project was originally developed using GDevelop. However, due to limited development time and local constraints, I transitioned to an AI-assisted development workflow.

This helped me:

  • Accelerate development
  • Improve existing design elements
  • Implement core gameplay systems
  • Integrate the main features
  • Complete a functional Minimum Viable Product (MVP)

NASA statistics and real-world spaceflight concepts informed the simulation's numerical values and events. Some values were simplified to keep the game educational and accessible.

Creativity and Innovation

SMIDGE combines two aspects of space exploration that are often treated separately:

  1. Spacecraft engineering: Designing a station and selecting its systems.
  2. Astronaut operations: Managing the station and responding to emergencies.

Players don't just design a station and receive a score. They actually experience the environment their engineering decisions create.

A station that looks good on paper may struggle when resources become limited or unexpected emergencies occur.

Factors Considered

Several factors influenced the game's design:

  • Realism: Using concepts inspired by the ISS and actual spaceflight.
  • Resource limitations: Setting restrictions on mass, power, and budget.
  • Crew survival: Making life-support systems essential.
  • System dependencies: Connecting equipment choices to station performance.
  • Unexpected events: Adding emergencies that challenge the original design.
  • Accessibility: Simplifying complex engineering concepts.
  • Replayability: Using different equipment combinations and random events to create different outcomes.

Overall Goal

SMIDGE demonstrates that successful space exploration requires more than reaching orbit. It requires careful engineering, resource management, adaptability, and the ability to maintain a safe environment for the crew.
